title: 口语专项：日常问答与两分钟展开 · Four listening sections
instructions: 原创模拟训练材料；先独立作答，再核对依据。四节音频共40题，按顺序听音作答。合成训练音频时长不同于正式考试。
transcript:
Section 1: Week 47 Listening: A Community Cooking Class

Mia: Hi, Tom! I heard you joined a cooking class last month. How’s it going?
Tom: Hey, Mia. Yes, I did. It’s actually really fun. I was a bit nervous at first because I hadn’t cooked much before, but now I look forward to it every week.
Mia: That’s great. What do you cook there?
Tom: Well, last week we made a vegetable curry. It was the first time I’d used so many spices. The teacher, Chef Anna, showed us how to balance the flavours. She said, “Don’t be afraid to taste as you go.” That advice really helped.
Mia: Sounds delicious. Is the class big?
Tom: Not really. There are only eight students, so we get a lot of attention. Most of them are beginners like me, but one woman, Lisa, has been cooking for years. She often helps others when the teacher is busy.
Mia: Nice. Do you have to bring your own ingredients?
Tom: No, everything is provided. The fee covers the ingredients and equipment. We just need to bring an apron and a notebook. Oh, and we have to arrive ten minutes early to set up.
Mia: How long is each session?
Tom: Two hours. We start at 6:30 p.m. and finish at 8:30. But last week we finished a bit late because the curry took longer than expected. Chef Anna said it was fine.
Mia: What do you enjoy most?
Tom: I think it’s the friendly atmosphere. Everyone chats and laughs while cooking. Also, I’ve learned to be more patient. Before, I used to rush and make mistakes. Now I take my time and the food tastes better.
Mia: Have you made anything at home?
Tom: Yes, I tried the curry recipe for my family last weekend. My mum said it was a bit too spicy, so next time I’ll use less chilli. But they liked it overall.
Mia: That’s a good start. Will you continue after this course?
Tom: Definitely. The course runs for six weeks, and we’re in week four now. After that, there’s an advanced class, but I think I’ll practise more at home first. Maybe I’ll join the advanced class next term.
Mia: Good plan. Oh, one more thing—can anyone join the class?
Tom: You need to be at least 18, and you have to book online. There’s a waiting list, but it’s not too long. Actually, you should try it, Mia. You’d enjoy it.
Mia: Maybe I will. Thanks, Tom!

Section 2: Community Garden Q&A Session

Mia: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for coming to our monthly community garden meeting. I'm Mia, the volunteer coordinator. Today, I'll answer some common questions about the garden. We've had several new members join recently, so I thought it would be useful to go over the basics for everyone, especially since many of you are new to the area and may not know how things work here.

Tom: Hi Mia, I'm Tom. I've just moved here. Can you tell me when the garden is open?

Mia: Sure, Tom. The garden is open every day from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. But on Sundays, we close at 4 p.m. for maintenance.

Tom: Great, thanks. And do I need to pay to join?

Mia: Yes, there's a small annual fee. It's £10 per person, or £15 for a family. That covers seeds and tools.

Lisa: Hello, I'm Lisa. I have two kids. Are children allowed to help?

Mia: Absolutely! We welcome families. Children under 12 must come with an adult. We also have a special children's plot where they can plant easy vegetables like carrots and beans.

Lisa: That's wonderful. What about the rules for using tools?

Mia: Good question. You must return all tools to the shed after use. And please clean them before putting them back. We also ask that you don't take tools home.

Tom: I see. Is there a waiting list for plots?

Mia: Yes, currently there is a waiting list of about three months. But you can join our workshops while you wait. They are free for members.

Lisa: What kind of workshops do you run?

Mia: We have workshops on composting, pruning, and seed saving. The next one is on composting this Saturday at 10 a.m. in the garden shed.

Tom: Do I need to bring anything?

Mia: Just gloves and a notebook. We provide all other materials.

Lisa: How can I sign up for the workshop?

Mia: You can sign up by sending an email to garden@community.org. Or you can call 555-1234. But email is faster.

Tom: Thanks, Mia. One last thing: is there a newsletter?

Mia: Yes, we send out a monthly newsletter with tips and event news. You'll receive it automatically once you become a member.

Lisa: Perfect. Thank you for the information.

Mia: You're welcome. I'm glad to help. Let's make our garden grow together!

Section 3: Week 47 Listening: Academic Discussion on a Group Project

TUTOR: Good morning, both of you. Thanks for coming. So, how is your group project on urban green spaces going?
STUDENT A (Mia): Well, we've collected quite a lot of data already. We interviewed twenty residents last week.
STUDENT B (Leo): Actually, Mia, it was twenty-two. Two more people joined at the last minute.
Mia: Oh right, twenty-two. Sorry. And we also took photos of three parks.
TUTOR: Good. And what have you found so far?
Leo: Most people said they use the park for exercise, but a few mentioned they go there to relax. One person said she goes to meet friends.
TUTOR: Interesting. Have you thought about how you'll present the data?
Mia: We were thinking of using charts, but Leo suggested a table might be clearer for the interview results.
Leo: Yes, because the numbers are small. A table shows the exact counts.
TUTOR: That's a reasonable point. But remember, your audience will be your classmates. They might find a chart more engaging. Perhaps you could use both: a chart for the overall trend and a table for details.
Mia: That's a good idea. We'll do that.
TUTOR: Now, what about the literature review? Have you found enough sources?
Leo: We've got five articles, but two of them are quite old—from the 1990s. We're not sure if they're still relevant.
TUTOR: Old sources can still be useful if they provide historical context. But you should also look for more recent studies. Try the university library database; it has a good selection.
Mia: Okay, we'll search there. Also, we're struggling with the conclusion. We don't know how to summarise our findings without repeating everything.
TUTOR: A good conclusion should not introduce new information. Instead, it should highlight the main patterns and maybe suggest one or two areas for further research. For example, you could mention that your sample was small, so future studies could include more participants.
Leo: That makes sense. So we could say that while most people use the park for exercise, a larger study might reveal different trends.
TUTOR: Exactly. Now, when is your presentation?
Mia: In two weeks, on the fifteenth.
TUTOR: And how long will it be?
Leo: About ten minutes, plus five minutes for questions.
TUTOR: Good. Make sure you practise timing. Also, decide who will speak about which part. Mia, you're good at explaining methods, so perhaps you could cover that. Leo, you could present the findings.
Mia: Sure. And we'll both handle the questions.
TUTOR: Perfect. One more thing: have you considered the ethical side? You interviewed people, so you need to ensure their responses are anonymous.
Leo: Yes, we didn't record names. We used numbers instead.
TUTOR: Excellent. Well, it sounds like you're on track. Keep me updated.

Section 4: The Art of the Follow-Up: Extending Answers in Conversation

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about a skill that many advanced learners find surprisingly difficult: extending answers in everyday conversation. You might think that once you can speak fluently, keeping a conversation going is easy. But in fact, even C1 speakers sometimes give short answers that stop the dialogue. So let's look at how to give a two-minute answer that feels natural.

First, let me explain what I mean by a two-minute answer. It's not about speaking for exactly two minutes. It's about having enough content to keep the other person interested. A good extended answer usually has three parts: a direct answer, a reason, and an example. For instance, if someone asks, "Do you enjoy cooking?" you could say, "Yes, I do. I find it relaxing after work. For example, last night I made a simple pasta dish and it helped me unwind." That's a direct answer, a reason, and an example.

Now, why do people give short answers? Often, it's because they are nervous or they think the other person is not interested. But in English-speaking cultures, asking follow-up questions is a sign of politeness. So if you give a short answer, the other person might think you don't want to talk. Therefore, extending your answer is a way to show you are friendly and engaged.

Another important point is using narrative tenses. When you give an example, you often need to tell a small story. For example, "Last week, I was walking in the park when I met an old friend. We hadn't seen each other for years, so we stopped and chatted." Here, the past continuous "was walking" sets the scene, and the past perfect "hadn't seen" shows an earlier event. Using these tenses correctly makes your story clear and interesting.

Descriptive clauses also help. Instead of saying "I met a friend," you can say "I met a friend who I hadn't seen since university." The clause "who I hadn't seen since university" adds detail and keeps the listener engaged. Similarly, you can use "which" or "where" to add information about things or places.

Finally, let's talk about reducing basic errors. Common mistakes include using present tense when telling a past story, or forgetting to use articles. For example, saying "I go to park yesterday" instead of "I went to the park yesterday." These errors can distract the listener. So practice your narrative tenses and articles until they become automatic.

To sum up, extending answers is a skill that requires practice. Use the direct answer, reason, and example structure. Use narrative tenses and descriptive clauses to add detail. And reduce basic errors by practicing regularly. Thank you.

grammar.title: 叙事时态、描述从句、原因与例子
grammar.explanation: 在口语中描述过去经历时，常用一般过去时和过去完成时（如 had cooked）来表示更早的动作。描述事物时可用定语从句（如 who has been cooking for years）来补充信息。表达原因可用 because，举例可用 like 或 for example。注意避免基础错误，如动词时态一致、主谓一致。
grammar.example: I was a bit nervous at first because I hadn’t cooked much before.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
options: She has been cooking for years.
She have been cooking for years.
answers: She has been cooking for years.
questions.explanation: 主语 She 是第三人称单数，现在完成进行时用 has been + 动词-ing。
questions.evidence: She has been cooking for years.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
options: I hadn’t cooked much before I joined the class.
I didn’t cooked much before I joined the class.

answers: I hadn’t cooked much before I joined the class.
questions.explanation: 过去完成时用 had + 过去分词，表示在过去的某个时间点之前已经完成的动作。
questions.evidence: I hadn’t cooked much before

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
options: The teacher, who is very patient, helps us a lot.
The teacher, who are very patient, helps us a lot.
The teacher, which is very patient, helps us a lot.
The teacher, whom is very patient, helps us a lot.
answers: The teacher, who is very patient, helps us a lot.
questions.explanation: 定语从句中，先行词是人时用 who，谓语与先行词一致。
questions.evidence: The teacher, Chef Anna, showed us how to balance the flavours.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
options: I was nervous because I hadn’t cooked before.
I was nervous because I didn’t cooked before.
I was nervous because I hadn’t cook before.
I was nervous because I haven’t cooked before.
answers: I was nervous because I hadn’t cooked before.
questions.explanation: because 引导原因状语从句，过去完成时用 had + 过去分词。
questions.evidence: I was a bit nervous at first because I hadn’t cooked much before
